topic: whether remote work should be a legal right
instructions: use no sentence longer than twenty words
use an em-dash-free, semicolon-free punctuation style
write the final paragraph in second person throughout
text:
Digital tools have changed how people work, yet laws lag behind this shift.
Some claim remote access is merely an employer gift they can withhold at will.
I argue instead that knowledge workers deserve a legal right to choose their location.
Denying this choice violates basic bodily autonomy and worsens inequality across the workforce.

Old labor laws protected bodies in factories, not minds connected via screens.
Today's economy relies on digital output where geography matters little for productivity.
Codifying remote work acknowledges that home offices support mental health better than many desks do.
When bosses reject hybrid schedules without real need, they treat workers as property to control physically.
This changes employment from a time exchange into a true value-for-value transaction between professionals.

Enshrining these rights helps promote equity and diversity in hiring practices today.
Talented people often lose jobs due to geography rather than lack of skill or ambition.
Requiring proximity to city hubs traps low-income workers where housing costs crush them.
A legal right lets rural families join the global economy without losing quality life.

Critics worry about supervision and culture, yet these are managerial problems solvable by trust strategies.
Better metrics replace surveillance that invades privacy unnecessarily.
Bosses who ban remote work want to control process instead of focusing on outcomes produced daily.

You see how freedom from discrimination is non-negotiable in our modern legal landscape today.
Safe working conditions remain a fundamental standard we cannot ignore regardless of industry sector changes now.
Flexible environments must become just such a recognized right in this digital age quickly enough.
Stop viewing remote work as optional convenience; treat it as essential for fair labor instead always.
